# Fair Ranking in RAG: Is the Benefit Fairness, or Diversity in Disguise?

*Working draft for content review — plain text, no LaTeX yet. Revised after
reviewer round 1 — see change notes marked with 🔧.*

*Idan Peretz, Avi Simkin.*

---

## The question this project set out to answer

The source paper this project extends (Kim & Diaz, "Towards Fair RAG")
reports that RAG systems built on fair, item-exposure-equalizing rankings
can, in many cases, preserve or improve the generation quality of systems
ranked purely by relevance, despite the usual expectation that enforcing
fairness costs ranking quality.

We didn't take that at face value. The specific fairness mechanisms that
tend to get used in practice — Plackett-Luce (PL) stochastic reranking,
which we use here — don't just make rankings fairer; as a side effect,
randomizing which relevant items get shown also tends to change how varied
the shown item set is. If a RAG generator benefits from seeing more varied
context, an observed "fairness helped" result could really be that variety
doing the work. So before believing fairness itself helps, you have to
first check whether its usual side effect — diversity — is the real cause.

That's the question this project asks: **when a fair ranking method seems
to help (or hurt) a RAG system's output quality, is that fairness, or is it
the diversity that fairness happens to produce?**

## Why this is hard to test directly

🔧 PL introduces stochasticity into the ranked candidate set according to
transformed retrieval scores, which redistributes expected exposure across
repeated rankings — that redistribution *can* increase how different the
shown items are from each other, as a byproduct. (Corrected: PL's sampler
isn't restricted to a known-relevant subset; it's the *fairness target* —
comparable-merit items receiving comparable exposure — that concerns
relevance, not the sampling mechanism itself.) But "fairness" here means
**expected exposure equality across repeated rankings**, and "diversity"
means **within-list textual variety in a single ranking** — two genuinely
different quantities that are not guaranteed to move together. 🔧 *(We
originally asserted they rise and fall together "by construction" — that
was an unearned assumption; see the empirical check below.)*

What lets us separate them at all is Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR): a
reranking method with an explicit relevance-vs-diversity dial and **no
fairness objective whatsoever**. Comparing PL to MMR after adjusting for
diversity level can tell us whether PL's outcomes track diversity alone, or whether
something is left over once diversity is accounted for — though, as
discussed below, that residual isn't automatically "the causal effect of
fairness," since PL and MMR differ in other ways too (stochastic vs.
deterministic, how each preserves the original relevance ordering, etc.).

## Setup

LaMP benchmark, all 7 tasks, "user" split. 🔧 *We use the full available
query set per task from the generator-dependent, per-generator-filtered
utility-label test collections this codebase's data pipeline builds from
the source paper's release (not an additional subsample drawn on top of
that filtering).* Two generators (Flan-T5-Small, 77M; Flan-T5-Base, 250M),
two retrievers (BM25, Contriever), top-*k* = 5 documents, 12 rerank
settings per cell: 1 relevance-only baseline, MMR at 7 diversity levels
(λ = 0.15–1.0), PL at 4 fairness strengths (α = 1, 2, 4, 8; **10 samples
per α**).

🔧 **Deviation from the source paper, stated explicitly:** the source paper
estimates its stochastic-ranking quantities (EE-D, EU under PL) from
*N* = 100 sampled rankings; we use *N* = 10, a computational compromise
given available hardware. This means our PL-based EE-D/EU estimates carry
more Monte Carlo noise than the source paper's. We treat this as a
limitation (Limitations, below), not something the current results correct
for.

Fairness: Expected Exposure disparity (EE-D, lower = fairer). 🔧 *We use the
source paper's own normalized EE-D directly (their pipeline computes it
against theoretical per-query bounds; we call `expeval.run(...,
normalize=True)` from their vendored code unchanged) — we do not apply any
further normalization to it ourselves.* Generation quality: Expected
Utility (EU — task-specific: accuracy for LaMP-1/2, MAE for LaMP-3,
ROUGE-L for LaMP-4–7). Diversity: ILD-Jaccard (1 − mean pairwise similarity
of retrieved profile text).

🔧 **Utility normalization, corrected and re-verified against the actual
code (round-1 wording was imprecise about the mechanism):** what we call
EU$_{norm}$ — our own within-query normalized utility, distinct from the
source paper's separate empirical-upper-bound normalization — is computed
as **true max-normalization**: for each query, divide its raw EU by the
single largest raw EU that query achieved across its 12 settings. (LaMP-3's
MAE, lower-is-better, is flipped via `4.0 − value` first so "higher =
better" holds everywhere before that division.) This is division by a
maximum, not min-max scaling — the denominator is exactly 0, and the
normalized value undefined, **only when every single one of a query's 12
settings scored raw EU = 0** (verified directly: all 237 affected queries
have raw EU = 0 in literally all 12 settings, no exceptions). That drops
5,688 of 163,392 rows (3.5%), concentrated in LaMP-1/2/5/6 (zero in
LaMP-3/7) — these are queries no method could get *any* credit on, not
queries where methods tied at a nonzero, informative value.

**Sensitivity check, run directly rather than left as a documentation
caveat:** since these are "zero for every setting" queries, we re-ran the
three headline regressions with them included (normalized EU filled at 0.0
instead of excluded) rather than dropped, to check whether exclusion was
inflating the estimated effects. Coefficients moved only slightly and all
three conclusions were unaffected — Finding 2's PL-only coefficient goes
from +0.0735 to +0.0697 (still p < 10⁻⁵⁰); Finding 3's from −0.0675 to
−0.0838 (significance *improves*, p = 0.012 → p = 0.0017); Finding 4's from
−0.0193 to −0.0188 (still p < 10⁻³³). We report the drop version throughout
as the primary numbers since it's the more conservative choice, but the
exclusion is not doing hidden work for any finding.

| LaMP task | flanT5Base queries | flanT5Small queries |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 232 | 51 |
| 2 | 280 | 192 |
| 3 | 378 | 311 |
| 4 | 827 | 833 |
| 5 | 759 | 826 |
| 6 | 783 | 760 |
| 7 | 211 | 365 |

336 total experiment runs, 163,392 query-level observations before the
normalization exclusion above.

**Sanity check:** MMR at λ = 1 removes the diversity term entirely and
should reproduce the deterministic ranking exactly. Checked directly on
this data: **0.0 maximum difference in EU across all 13,616 paired
queries** — confirmed, not assumed.

---

## 🔧 Testing the premise: does PL's fairness mechanism actually increase diversity here?

Before treating "PL trades off fairness against diversity together" as
given, we checked it directly rather than asserting it.

**Row-level correlation is weak:** Pearson r(EE-D_norm, ILD_norm) within PL
rows = **−0.086** (n = 54,464) — a small effect once you look query-by-
query, swamped by per-query noise in both quantities.

**But the aggregate, by-α pattern is clean and monotonic:**

| PL α (lower = fairer) | mean EE-D (raw) | mean ILD-Jaccard (raw) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.210 | 0.879 |
| 2 | 0.248 | 0.870 |
| 4 | 0.657 | 0.838 |
| 8 | 0.948 | 0.830 |

As α increases (fairness weakens toward the deterministic baseline),
disparity rises and diversity falls, in lockstep. So the premise holds *in
aggregate, as a tendency across the fairness dial* — it does not hold as a
tight per-query coupling. We report both: the mechanism the project's
design leans on is real but loose, not a strict "by construction"
guarantee, and that looseness is itself part of why PL vs. MMR "adjusted
for ILD" isn't a clean causal isolation (see Finding 4).

---

## Finding 1 — Fairness essentially doesn't pay off

![fig1 — deterministic-baseline generation quality per task (normalized EU)](data:image/png;base64,)

*fig1 — deterministic-baseline generation quality per task, normalized EU
(🔧 previously raw EU, which isn't comparable across LaMP's different
metrics — fixed).*

🔧 **Scoped to PL only, since Finding 1's headline is specifically about
fairness — MMR has no fairness objective, so it doesn't belong in a test
about whether fairness pays off** (round-1's version pooled 16 PL and 8 MMR
comparisons into one "24 tests" family; the MMR comparisons now live in
Finding 3, where they're evidence about diversity instead). Testing each
PL α against the relevance-only baseline (paired, per-query, Holm-corrected
within each cell's 4-test family: 4 α values × 4 cells = 16 tests total):

**10 of 16 are statistically significant, and 8 of those are losses.** Two
are gains — both the same PL configuration (α = 4) in two different cells
— but tiny (+0.0014 and +0.0025 in normalized EU) against losses an order
of magnitude larger elsewhere.

🔧 The source paper's own conclusion is more nuanced than "fair rankings
often outperform" — it reports an overall fairness/quality tradeoff with
moderate fairness settings sometimes preserving or improving utility. Given
we test 2 of their 4 generators, 2 of 3 retrievers, and *N*=10 vs. their
*N*=100: **within the two smaller generators and two retrievers evaluated
here, we do not reproduce the pattern that moderate fair reranking
frequently preserves or improves deterministic-baseline utility** — the
direction is overwhelmingly negative, with two small, real, but practically
negligible exceptions.

## Finding 2 — A real fairness-utility tradeoff, within PL's own fairness dial

![fig2 — EE-D vs. EU per setting](data:image/png;base64,)

*fig2 — EE-D vs. EU per setting, PL path traced across α, one panel per
cell.*

🔧 **This regression is now scoped to PL rows only** — pooling PL with MMR
and deterministic rows (as we did before) mixes a within-method fairness
manipulation (PL's α) with a between-method contrast (MMR/deterministic
sit at a fixed EE-D ≈ 1 regardless of λ), which isn't a clean fairness-
dial estimate. Within PL alone: **coefficient(EE-D) = +0.0735** — larger
than the earlier all-rows estimate (+0.0533), not smaller. 🔧 **Inference
also now accounts for each query appearing multiple times** (once per α,
per retriever) — cluster-robust by query: **p = 6.3×10⁻⁵⁴** (n = 52,568,
4,269 query clusters) — down from the naive p = 2.1×10⁻⁹³ that treated
repeated observations of the same query as independent, but still
overwhelmingly significant.

🔧 Leave-one-task-out, rerun on the same PL-only specification as the
coefficient above (classical SEs, for comparability with the robustness
figure): the coefficient stays positive and highly significant (p < 10⁻⁴²
in every case) across all seven single-task drops — range +0.0613 (dropping
LaMP-4) to +0.0834 (dropping LaMP-5), versus +0.0735 for the full PL-only
sample. No sign flips, no significance flips; the association is not being
driven by any single LaMP task.

## Finding 3 — Diversity's own effect: real, but weaker than it first looked

If diversity were secretly what makes fairness look good, diversity should
help on its own, holding fairness constant (MMR, which has no fairness
mechanism at all). 🔧 It doesn't — but "diversity actively hurts" overstates
the evidence too. More precisely: **we find no evidence of a general
utility benefit from increased MMR diversity; the pooled association is
modestly negative, but heterogeneous across tasks and model
configurations.**

![fig4 — within-MMR association between diversity and utility, per cell](data:image/png;base64,)

*fig4 — within-MMR regression of EU on ILD, per cell, exposure disparity
fixed at the deterministic level (EE-D = 1) since MMR has no fairness
mechanism. 🔧 (Title/caption corrected — the previous version claimed
"diversity's harm fades with generator size," which is backwards: the
per-cell coefficients shown are Small/BM25 ≈ −0.037, Small/Contriever ≈
−0.015, Base/BM25 ≈ −0.148, Base/Contriever ≈ −0.073 — Base's effect is
*larger* in magnitude, not smaller, for both rankers.)*

Pooled: **coefficient(ILD) = −0.0675** (n = 91,994). 🔧 With cluster-robust
(by-query) inference, **p = 0.0115** — real, but a much more modest
significance level than the naive p = 5.6×10⁻¹⁰ suggested; the repeated-
query structure was meaningfully inflating confidence here specifically.

Leave-one-task-out: the pooled coefficient stays negative for every task
dropped (classical SEs). 🔧 That establishes the pooled result isn't
carried by any single task — it does **not** establish the effect is
negative in every task, and it isn't: two tasks, LaMP-2 and LaMP-5, show a
*positive* coefficient when fit on their own data alone. So: **the pooled
negative association is robust to removing any one task, but the direction
is heterogeneous across tasks** — diversity's effect looks benchmark-
dependent, not a fixed property of RAG generation.

🔧 The figure also suggests the negative association is stronger for the
larger generator. Descriptively, that holds: per-cell cluster-robust
coefficients are Small/BM25 −0.0025 (p=0.95, not significant),
Small/Contriever −0.0334 (p=0.36, not significant), Base/BM25 **−0.1371
(p=1.8×10⁻⁴, significant)**, Base/Contriever **−0.0930 (p=0.013,
significant)** — Base's cells are individually significant and Small's are
not. But the formal test of that pattern — a pooled within-MMR regression
with an ILD×generator interaction term, cluster-robust by query — puts the
Small-vs-Base difference itself at only **p = 0.28, not significant**
(n = 91,994, 4,269 clusters). We report both: the descriptive per-cell
split is real and visible in fig4, but we don't have the power to formally
confirm generator size as the driver of it.

🔧 A complementary check: does MMR ever significantly beat or lose to the
deterministic baseline on its own (not the ILD-slope regression above, but
a direct paired test)? Across the 4 cells × 2 λ values used in Finding 1's
family (Holm-corrected within each cell), **3 of 8 are significant, and
all 3 are losses** (largest: flanT5Small/Contriever at λ=0.15, Δ = −0.0265,
p<10⁻⁴); 6 of 8 point negative overall, 2 of 8 (both at the weaker λ=0.55)
point slightly positive but not significantly. MMR does not show a
significant utility win over deterministic ranking in any of the 8
settings tested.

## Finding 4 — PL has a residual utility disadvantage relative to MMR after adjusting for ILD

🔧 *(Renamed from "Fairness's own mechanism carries a cost diversity
doesn't explain" — that framing claimed more identification than this
design supports; see below.)*

🔧 Take only the PL and MMR rows, add measured ILD as a regression
covariate, and ask whether being a PL setting (vs. MMR) predicts a further
utility difference at comparable measured ILD. ("Matched diversity"
language has been replaced throughout this section — this is a regression
adjustment, not a matching procedure.)

![fig7 — EU by diversity level, PL vs. MMR, ILD-adjusted](data:image/png;base64,)

*fig7 — EU by diversity level, PL vs. MMR, ILD-adjusted.*

| Cell | coef(is_PL), net of ILD | p |
|---|---|---|
| flanT5Small / BM25 | −0.0130 | 1.1×10⁻⁴ |
| flanT5Base / BM25 | −0.0226 | 8.2×10⁻¹¹ |
| flanT5Small / Contriever | −0.0186 | 4.7×10⁻⁸ |
| flanT5Base / Contriever | −0.0227 | 1.3×10⁻¹⁰ |

All four cells negative, significant, similar magnitude (pooled coef =
−0.0194; cluster-robust p = 8.8×10⁻³⁴ — this one *strengthens*, not
weakens, under cluster-robust inference).

🔧 **What this does and doesn't establish.** Adjusting for ILD controls for
one measured outcome of the ranking, not for everything that differs
between PL and MMR — PL is stochastic and MMR deterministic, they may
preserve the original relevance ordering differently, and PL introduces
variance across repeated draws that MMR doesn't have. So this coefficient
is an **average adjusted difference between PL and MMR after controlling
for measured ILD** — not a clean causal estimate of "what fairness itself
costs," and not evidence that PL underperforms at *every* diversity level:
fig7 shows individual ILD bins where that isn't the case. We originally described this as "isolating fairness's contribution
beyond diversity"; that overstated what the design identifies, and we've
corrected the framing.

**We tested our own proposed mechanism, and it did not hold up.** Our
working hypothesis was that PL pays a *relevance* cost — stochastic
sampling moves away from the highest-ranked item, and that specifically
(not diversity) explains the residual. The source paper's EE-R metric
(exposure alignment with useful items) is a direct proxy for this. Adding
EE-R as a covariate: coef(is_PL) moves from −0.0194 to **−0.0187** —
essentially unchanged (EE-R itself is strongly associated with EU,
coef = +0.158, p ≈ 0, a reassuring sanity check that EE-R behaves as
expected — it just doesn't explain away PL's residual). **The relevance-
cost story is not confirmed by this test.** The honest conclusion is
narrower than what we originally wrote: PL underperforms MMR on average
after adjusting for ILD, robustly, and the mechanism for *why* remains open — plausible
candidates include the stochasticity itself (variance, not just a mean
shift) or something ILD and EE-R together don't capture, but we have not
demonstrated which.

## Robustness

Every coefficient above was checked leave-one-task-out; none depend on any
single task remaining in the sample. 🔧 Cluster-robust (by-query) inference
was added to correct for repeated observations of the same query across
settings — it changes exact significance levels (most notably Finding 3,
where it moves from p = 5.6×10⁻¹⁰ to p = 0.0115) but does not overturn any
finding's direction or overall conclusion.

## Limitations

- **Scale.** Whether this tradeoff grows, shrinks, or reverses at generator
  scales beyond 250M parameters is untested — utility labels exist for a
  much larger (XXL) generator, but it doesn't fit the GPU available for
  this project.
- **PL sample count.** *N* = 10 vs. the source paper's *N* = 100 — our
  PL-based EE-D/EU estimates carry more Monte Carlo noise than theirs. A
  cheap follow-up (recomputing EE-D only at N=100 on a subset, no
  generation needed) would bound how much this matters but hasn't been
  run yet.
- **EE-D and ILD are conceptually different quantities** (exposure equality
  across repeated rankings vs. within-list textual variety) that are only
  loosely, not strictly, coupled under PL in this data (see the premise
  check above) — this limits how cleanly ILD-adjusted comparisons can
  isolate anything.
- **Task dependence.** Findings 2 and 3's pooled effects are LOTO-robust,
  but individual tasks (LaMP-7 for the tradeoff; LaMP-2, LaMP-5 for
  diversity) go the other way on their own — both effects look
  benchmark-shaped rather than universal.

## Bottom line

🔧 In our Flan-T5-Small/Base experiments (2 of the source paper's 4
generators, 2 of 3 retrievers, *N*=10 vs. their *N*=100), we do not find
evidence that apparent utility gains from fair reranking are explained by
increased within-list diversity. PL reranking generally fails to improve
utility relative to deterministic retrieval (Finding 1); within PL's own
fairness dial, greater exposure equality is robustly associated with lower
utility (Finding 2); MMR-induced diversity has a real but modest pooled
negative association with utility, heterogeneous across tasks (Finding 3);
and after adjusting for ILD, PL still underperforms MMR on average
(Finding 4) — a residual gap that should **not** be read as "the causal
cost of fairness itself," since PL and MMR differ in more than diversity, and our own test
of the most obvious candidate mechanism (a relevance cost, via EE-R) did
not confirm it. What we can say cleanly: **diversity alone does not
account for the difference between how PL and MMR perform**, and further
work isolating *why* — likely requiring a design that varies fairness and
diversity independently, not just controls for one while measuring the
other — is the natural next step.
